title: Load Balancing — Layers & Algorithms
summary: L4 vs L7 load balancing and the concrete algorithms used to pick a backend, plus the health checking and stickiness that come with it.

slides.markdown:
A **load balancer** sits between clients and a pool of backend servers, spreading requests so no single server gets overwhelmed and failed servers get quietly routed around. Every service you've used at scale — search, checkout, a video feed — has one in front of it, even if you never see it.

- Distributes traffic across backends by some algorithm (round robin, least connections, ...).
- Operates at either the **connection level (L4)** or the **content level (L7)** — different trade-offs.
- Also does health checking: it stops sending traffic to a backend that's down.

![Clients hitting a load balancer, which distributes requests across a pool of backend servers](assets/lb-overview.svg)

Clients only ever know one address — the load balancer's. It decides, request by request or connection by connection, which backend actually handles the work, and the client never sees which one it was.

assets.alt: Clients hitting a load balancer, which distributes requests across a pool of backend servers

slides.markdown:
**Layer 4 (L4)** load balancing works at the connection level — it looks at IP address and port, not what's inside the packets, and forwards the whole TCP (or UDP) connection to a chosen backend. Once a connection is assigned, all its packets go to the same backend for the life of that connection.

It's fast because there's nothing to parse — no HTTP, no TLS to terminate — just routing based on network-layer info. That speed is the trade-off for flexibility: an L4 balancer can't route `/api/users` differently from `/api/orders`, because it never looks that far into the traffic.

**Layer 7 (L7)** load balancing terminates the actual protocol (usually HTTP) and reads its content — host header, URL path, cookies — before deciding where to send a request. That lets it route `api.example.com` to one pool and `static.example.com` to another, or split by path prefix.

The cost is real work per request: parsing HTTP (and usually TLS termination) takes CPU an L4 balancer never spends. Most modern web apps front with L7 (or a reverse proxy — see [reverse-proxies-gateways](reverse-proxies-gateways)) for that routing flexibility.

| | L4 | L7 |
|---|---|---|
| Sees | IP + port | Full HTTP request (headers, path, cookies) |
| Routing granularity | Whole connection | Per-request, by content |
| CPU cost | Very low | Higher — parses/terminates protocol |
| Typical use | Raw TCP services, extreme scale | Web apps, API routing, microservices |

**How to decide:** need to route by URL path, host, or cookie? You need L7. Pushing millions of simple connections with no content-aware routing need? L4 is cheaper and simpler.

The load balancer still needs a rule to pick *which* backend. The common ones:

- **Round robin** — cycle through backends in order. Simple, assumes equal capacity.
- **Weighted round robin** — like round robin, but stronger backends get proportionally more requests.
- **Least connections** — send to whichever backend has the fewest active connections; adapts to uneven request duration.
- **IP hash** — hash the client IP to consistently pick the same backend, a crude form of stickiness.

None is universally best — round robin suits uniform, short requests; least connections shines when duration varies a lot.

**Consistent hashing** solves a specific problem: IP-hash-style routing (hash mod N) reshuffles almost every key's assignment the moment N changes — add or remove one backend, and most clients get remapped, thrashing any per-server cache or session state.

Consistent hashing maps backends and keys onto a **ring**; a key goes to the next backend clockwise from it. Adding or removing one backend only reassigns keys between it and its neighbor — everything else keeps its mapping. This is what lets CDNs and caches add/remove nodes without a global reshuffle.

A load balancer is only as good as its view of which backends are alive:

- **Active health checks** — the balancer periodically pings backends (e.g. `GET /health` every 5s) and pulls one out of rotation on repeated failure.
- **Passive health checks** — the balancer watches real traffic; if a backend starts erroring or timing out live, it's marked unhealthy without a dedicated probe.

Production systems run both: active checks catch a dead backend before real traffic hits it; passive checks catch failures a shallow health endpoint doesn't reveal.

slides.subTitle: L7 routing by path
slides.markdown:
![An L7 load balancer routing /api requests to an API pool and /static requests to a static-file pool](assets/lb-path-routing.svg)

The load balancer inspects each request's path *after* the connection and (if HTTPS) TLS are already established, then forwards it to whichever backend pool matches — something an L4 balancer structurally cannot do, since it never parses the request line.

assets.alt: An L7 load balancer routing /api requests to an API pool and /static requests to a static-file pool

slides.markdown:
Some apps store session state **in the memory of the specific server** that first handled a user — **session persistence** keeps routing that user to the same backend, usually via a cookie or IP hash.

It complicates scaling: a sticky backend can't be drained instantly (in-flight users lose state), and uneven stickiness can leave one backend overloaded. It's especially awkward for WebSocket-heavy apps, pinned for a connection's whole duration — see [websockets-realtime](websockets-realtime). The cleaner fix is externalizing session state (Redis) so any backend serves any request.

slides.subTitle: Least-connections and unequal capacity
slides.markdown: A tempting default: **always use least-connections, it adapts automatically.** It doesn't account for **unequal backend capacity** — if one server has half the CPU of the others, least-connections will still send it just as many connections as a stronger backend, because it only counts *connections*, not the load each one represents. The fix is **weighted least-connections**, factoring in each backend's actual capacity — plain least-connections silently assumes every backend is identical.
